projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edmund Kuivila was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: In 1941, I was living at 507 6th Street, Fairport Harbor, Ohio. That's where I was born. And that was at the house that my dad built. And there were nine of us kids living there. Nine children, five boys and four girls, and I was the baby. Youngest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: In 1941, I was 21 years old. I was born -- wait a minute, I was 20 years old. I was born in 1921. So in 1941, I was 20 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you working or were you in school at that point?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: At that time, I was working. This was previous to going into the military, into the Army Air Corps. I was about to be drafted and I wanted to join the Air Corps, but my parents wouldn't let me sign up right away, see. But then when I got my draft notice, things changed. So I went to Cleveland and I enlisted. That way I was able to stay out of the military for about maybe three or four months longer. And I went into the service then, I think it was in -- what was it, November of 1942.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's when you signed up?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, that's -- I may have been called up after, you know, called up. Right, because after enlisting in the Army Air Corps, I stayed at home. They didn't call me up for probably about three months later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Backtracking just a second, do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Not too much. I remember it happening, you know, and all that. But as far as just anything special that transpired at that time, why I don't recall.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did many of your friends or anything sign up immediately?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, there were some that did. And as a matter of fact, you know, back then especially like our class -- our graduating class of Harding High School in Fairport, quite a number of those fellas either enlisted, they wanted to join the Air Corps, or the Naval Air Corps. Whichever, Army or Navy. And also then -- well, as time went on, they were drafted. Those who didn't enlist. There were quite a number of us that were in the military.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you went in in November of '42; right?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: In November of 1942, yes. I reported to Columbus and from there a number of us from the Ohio area were put on a train and shipped to Santa Ana, California. I think that trip took, I forget how many nights. I think about two or three days. We made a stop in -- what was it, maybe San Antonio, Texas. Somewhere over there. And I guess we picked up some more guys. Anyway we wound up at Santa Ana, California, for Army Air Corps training. I don't know whether it was basic, I forget what it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were -- were you mostly with guys from Ohio or were you thrown in with guys all from over the country?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, at that time, mostly guys from Ohio. But then when we started training, when we had gone into training there were guys from various parts of the country.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that a tough adjustment to adjust to guys from other parts of the country that you had never known before?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: No, not really, because we were, you know, all in the same boat. And just all of the guys, they were very friendly and we got along very well. No problems there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about your training, then?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, let's see now. First the -- when I reported to Santa Ana, California, why first we had what was called preflight and it was mostly schooling. And then from there, I went to gunnery school. I was a bombardier, so I went to gunnery school. And I spent I forget how much time. This took place in Kingman, Arizona, as I recall. And after gunnery school, why then I went to bombardier school in Deming, New Mexico, and got my commission on December 24th of 1943 -- I believe it was '43. Yeah. And then got to come home for a short period of time, maybe about a week. And then I had to report to Salt Lake City, Utah, where we formed as a group. And then on to Kearney, Nebraska, and where we picked up a plane and flew that plane across the United States and then over into Scotland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was bombardier your choice? Is that the position you wanted?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, I first wanted to go into pilot training, but I didn't make it there. So anyway they offered me a chance to go to bombardier school. Some fellows who may have gone into pilot training and didn't make it, well, they were what we called them washed out, why, then they reverted back to the -- you might say the GI's, you know, the regular Air Force. Some of the stuff has kind of has faded from my mind, but I'm recalling it as best I can.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great. Anything before we get overseas, any other unusual stories from your training time?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, I'm trying to -- let's see -- I don't think of anything offhand. I do know that it was quite a long flight. We flew from Kearney, Nebraska, across country to -- what was it, New Hampshire. And then from there, we flew to Goose Bay, Labrador. And then when we landed in Goose Bay, Labrador, they had cleaned the runways off and the snow was piling at least -- at least 6 feet high on the side of the runways. And spent maybe two days there and from there we went to Scotland. No, I beg your pardon. Flew to Iceland. From Iceland to Scotland, and then that's when we left our planes and went by train to our group that we were going to be in. You know, I was in the 96th Bomber Group. And that's where I stayed, 413th Squadron, 96th Bomber Group.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you didn't keep the plane that you flew overseas with?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Oh, no, no, we left those planes in -- in Scotland and I don't know what they did with them there. I guess whatever groups did with planes, whether they were dispersed to various airfields.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you make this flight? Was that early '44?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, let's see. That was in 1944 -- goodness gracious.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't need the exact date. I just want to get a rough idea.

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, actually, I got my commission in December -- on December 24th, and so these flights that we made were -- well, first of all, of course we -- I got my commission -- I guess it was probably, I think it's in chronological order there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't say when, but obviously you were flying missions.

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Does it have a second page there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, do you remember when you flew your first mission?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Oh, some time in the spring of 1944.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly. You mentioned here a D-Day mission. What was life like in Great Britain when you got over there?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, I didn't get a chance to see much of life in Great Britain. I think we had one leave and on that leave it was just a matter of, I think, maybe about a day, two at the most. And I remember being in London and there was an air raid. We had to go down into an air raid shelter. And the thing that the Germans were sending over there at that time these buzz bombs. And you could hear them. It sounded like an airplane, a very different tone. And then you would hear the engines stop, that's when they would come down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you scared?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, that was the only time I had an experience with hearing anything like that. Because when we went to our base, I don't recall any attacks by the buzz bombs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have much contact with the British civilians?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Not too much, no. No, as a matter of fact, the first contact I had was when we were on the leave, you know, just a short time. And then I believe there were some British civilians working on the air base where we were stationed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were flying B-17s; right?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: I was a bombardier on a B-17. I will show you a picture of a B-17 that my son bought for me. It's a -- it's by a fellow, by an artist. And it's a very definitive representation of a B-17. You can even see -- it's got the rivets on it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your plane have a name?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: No, because actually we -- I was shot down. I was on the 11th mission when I was shot down. We were shot down. And the young fellas on our crew were just on their 10th, because I had flown as a bombardier on another mission with a different group. Different pilot. And different plane, I should say. I think their bombardier at that time may have been ill. Whatever the reason was, I don't know. So actually, I had one mission more than the other fellas on our plane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you flew in various planes?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yeah, most of the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first mission?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yeah, vaguely. We didn't come in contact with any German fighters. As a matter of fact the only time I saw any German fighters was on the day we were shot down. I think it was -- of course I was sitting up there in front with all of the glass. I could see everything ahead of us. And all the sudden I see this FW-190 come flying over. I had guns but I didn't even get the chance to get the guns up there to shoot at it. And I think that was probably the plane that had shot up our plane, our B-17, because we had, oh, I think two engines shot out and we lost one of the waist gunners. He got killed. The rest of us, I guess, we were okay because we all bailed out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why don't you go ahead and describe in detail, if you can, that mission. Was that flown on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Oh, no. That was that was two weeks, exactly two weeks after D-Day. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: After D-Day. Were there any other memorable missions before that mission?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, let's see. Yeah, there were. Because one of our longest mission was Magdeburg, Germany. And I don't know if I have got that on the paper or not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It looks like June 6th, 1944, railroad yard in Magdeburg, Germany?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: That was it. Yeah. And that's where we were shot down by flak mostly I think and maybe fighters too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was the 11th mission, then?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: That was my 11th mission, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your 11th mission?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: And what was that -- on what date?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It says June 6th, 1944.

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Oh, no, that was D-Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was D-Day. Describe that mission.

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, on that mission, things were pretty -- they were short missions. The only thing is that we were told before we took off, if you -- they had every darned plane that flew in the sky that day, you know. So it was early in the morning and we were making a lot of vapor trails, because as you made vapor trails you had to keep on going on up. And finally we were at about 30,000 feet when we lost our group, so they told us if you lose your group, tag on with somebody else. Which is what we did. And we went over, dropped our bombs, and there was a certain route that we had to follow across the channel in this one area here. But to come back, we had to cut across France to the west -- yeah, west. And then at a certain point, we had to come across and then into England. If we did not follow that pattern, why, "boom, boom, boom," by the Americans. They would shoot at us. And our second mission on that day, we flew two missions. The first was early in the morning and the second one was in the afternoon some time. And, well, I forget whether we lost our group that day -- that mission. But anyway before we got back to England, it was dark. And so we landed on an RAF air base. And they always flew at night. And on the air base, well, when we landed there, they had perimeter lights. You have to come in like this. The lights went around the field like this. A bunch of lights going around like that. If you came in anywhere else: Boom. They would shoot you down. And we were told that as we were coming in that they had plenty aircraft aimed at us just in case.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, they could spot what kind of plane it was though. Were they afraid that the Germans had commandeered a B-17?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: No, they weren't afraid of that. But they didn't know -- being dark, nighttime, they didn't know just I mean, for sure. And we spent the night there. They put us up in the RAF officers quarters. And in the morning when I woke up there was a cup of tea next to the bed. I don't know what time it was put there, because it was cold. And I think a crumpet or something like that. And they had taken my flying shoes which I had never touched to polish at all. They were leather. They were shoes about that high. And I wondered where the heck are they? And I looked outside the door and they were outside the door and they had been polished. So you can see what kind of care the RAF pilots got. So anyway then we -- I think we had some breakfast there and got in the plane and then flew back to our base.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a good crew? Did you get along with the guys in your crew?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Oh, yes we did. We had a good crew. As a matter of fact I have got a picture of the whole crew that I'll show you also. And this picture was taken -- I believe we were in England at the time, I'm sure. Because that's when -- let's see, I'm trying to think when we actually became a crew. I think that it may have been when we were in Kearney, Nebraska. So we formed our group there, 10 guys. And a pilot, copilot, navigator, bombardier, and the engineer, radio operator and a tail gunner, lower ball turret gunner, two waist gunners, ten guys all told.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any of them that was particularly close to you?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, I was probably -- you know, we, the four of us, the pilot, copilot, navigator and myself, we were officers, and the rest of them were enlisted men. But I used to say if we went in a pub some place and maybe the waist gunner or somebody came in there, we chatted. There was a camaraderie, naturally. And we would have a drink or they would buy me a drink. Although we didn't have that much time off, unfortunately.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other memorable missions before that mission where you were shot down?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, I can't think of anything outstanding or unique.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was mostly flak that you were dealing with, not so much fighters before that last mission?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: That last mission. That was the first time I saw any fighter attack. The way I knew it was a fighter attack, we would go like this in that FW-190 which would fly over. It was too fast.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and describe that mission where you were shot down. As much as you can remember about that.

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, we had dropped our bombs and we it turned off the target.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the target?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: That particular day, what was it? I don't know whether I had it written down. Maybe not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It doesn't say. All right?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: But anyway, it seemed to us what was going to be what we called a milk run. A milk run where we just had to fly across the channel like D-Day. Fly across and drop your bombs and come back home. Or else made where we meet any kind of fighter or anti-aircraft resistance. And -- but on that day, everything was going fine, until I guess -- I don't know whether we had left the target area, but "boom, boom, boom," you known, anti-aircraft fire. You could see the stuff bursting in the air, black puffs of smoke. As long as you saw that, you knew you weren't hit. They were down below because they were swirling upward. And so then on that day we were shot down everything seemed to go very well until I heard back there that somebody had been hit. I think it was our left waist gunner. He got killed. I don't know if anybody else got hit. But I know the fighters came in and like I mentioned they shot out two engines and our controls were shot. And so we were losing altitude and the pilot couldn't control the plane so he gave the order to bail out. So that's what we did. I strapped on my -- well, we always -- see we had chest -- chest packs. And I always had one hooked up right here so I would have to start reaching over and so I just swung it over and I got out the front end of the plane there. And there was an opening about maybe so wide, so big. The way we went out. You pulled your arms in and just tumbled out. Fell out. And eventually then I was falling on my back and I pulled the ripcord and it opened. And before I hit the ground, I could see all these -- they were Hitler youngsters, you know, but one officer. And we were drifting down with the currents. Drifting like this. And I could see those kids moving this way and that way on the ground. And then we landed and I just put up my hands. The kids didn't have any guns, but they had one an officer with them that did have a gun. So they kind of moved to what was their jail at the base. I must have landed fairly close to some kind of military installation, because we didn't have to walk very far before I was in the hoosgow over there. And that's when I spent I forget how long. And then one day we got a train and I think it was the pilot, copilot, navigator and me. We were on a train with a Nazi guy and we were transported to a gulag, which was a temporary prison camp. And then from there we went to a Stalag 3. It was actually in one of those -- Poland, which was territory which had been taken over by the Germans in their invasions. And so that's where we remained until the following -- following spring. When the Russians were advancing on the eastern front. And I believe this Stalag 3 was where we were, I believe that was in Polish territory. And so the Russians advanced and the Germans moved us out. One night, they came around and said we are moving out. They didn't tell us, but they told -- what we in the barracks called Creegie, in other words, you know, the fellow who went to the meetings with the power -- higher officers just to let us know what was going on with the Germans and all the Americans' demands and so forth and so on. And so anyway this guy came around and told us get ready to move out, we're leaving in one hour. It lasted longer than an hour. But you should have seen. All hell broke loose. Everybody storing their clothes into some kind of a bag or something like that. It was a cold winter night too. I forget, we took our blankets and put them over our heads and put a pin right here. So we went like that. Rain gear. And so they got us out and started marching us. And I forget whether it was the next day or when it was, why they put us on these box cars, what were called 40-and-8 boxcars during World War I. Forty men or eight horses, so you can imagine how big they were. Not very big. And I don't know how many guys, but there was barely room enough for us all to sit on the floor. And then -- then we had what we called a comfort stop where we would stop some place where there was wide open space and they would open the doors and the guys could run out into the fields to take a leak or have a beer. Because we couldn't do anything -- we did have a bucket that we used for a urinal. And I guess some of the guys tried to -- they may have tried to cut a hole in the boxcar so you could penis there and take a leak to the outside. I don't know whether that ever worked out. Those were some of the clear moments. And then, well, we got to this camp and they took us to Stalag 7A, which was down by Moosberg Germany, the southern part of Germany where which hadn't been invaded yet. But then it was in the spring, why, General Patton's army came through there and liberated us and all those German soldiers and guards, why, they took off somewhere. We saw the U.S. flag hoisted up on the headquarters. And then one -- one day, I think it was probably the next day, why, General Patton came through our barracks. The Germans had, one, two, three, I think they were about four bunks high. Straw mattresses. And at that time I was in my bunk which was the top bunk. And I hear somebody yell "ten-hut." And I wondered what is going on. And later I see this head bobbing by, you know. And I said who was that? General Patton. And there I was still in the bunk.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he say anything?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: No. I don't know whether he did because I was in the bunk and he walked through the barracks through in one door and out this door over here. I would like to have seen him, but I didn't know who he was. I thought maybe it was just a German or something like that, you know. So anyway then those were the guys who liberated us. And from there they took us by a truck to La Havre. In that area and we lived in tents. And they fed us pretty well. Twice a day they fed us eggnog to fatten us up and all that. And then I forget what day it was they took us to the channel and put us on the ship. It was regularly a German luxury liner, which the Americans had captured down in South America and then they worked it over and made a troop ship out of it. And so that thing, that's what we came back to the States on. First we cruised to England, crossed the channel to England and picked up some hospital cases and came across the ocean. And I forget how many days it took us to cross. And we landed in I think was it, Maryland, I guess? No, I'm not sure. Somewhere -- wherever we landed, why, we could see the Statue of Liberty to the east of us. And they didn't waste any time. They got us on the train and we went to Camp Atterbury. And there they processed us and gave us tickets home. I think I spent one night at Camp Atterbury and then the next day I caught a bus to Chicago and from Chicago I came back to Cleveland and my parents and my sister were waiting for me at -- it was a train station, they were waiting for me at the train station.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that meeting with your family like?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, it was kind of touching. Yeah. And then I think I had -- I think I had 90 days home, if I recall correctly. And then I had to report to down to Miami Beach, Florida, for about another month where they tried to -- you know, that was sort of like R&R down there. We lived in one of the ocean front hotels. I forget how many guys they had. I don't recall ever seeing any of them. But anyway, we had a swimming pool there and I went swimming every day. But you know the swimming pool, it had salt water in it because we were right on the ocean. That was really something. Salt water in the swimming pool. And then I didn't want to reenlist. I just wanted to get out of service and continue my life. And so I got my papers and train ticket and went home and that's when my parents met me at Cleveland terminal, that's the train station, you know, the terminal. And that's when -- then when I actually got out of service, why, the copilot from our crew, he had his car down in Miami Beach, and he gave me a ride to about Pittsburgh, and I think I caught a bus from there and went home on the bus. And I spent some time -- let's see that's when we came home all together. Came home and that was it. And then I don't know what year it was, the GIs were all getting free tuition in colleges, and so I spent one year at Denison University, Angola -- not Angola -- Denison, that's in Ohio. And I took some engineering courses and calculus and physics and sort of those things because I planned to get a degree in mechanical engineering, which they didn't have a full course in that so I transferred to Tri-State College in Angola, Indiana, and I got my degree from there. And that's about it from then on. Back to work.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit. Do have you any details about life in any of those prison camps?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, one of the things that stands out more probably than anything is that we didn't feel that we got a belly full -- you know, plenty of food to eat. They used to come around there were some enlisted men that worked in the kitchen over there in Stalag 3 where we were and they may come around in the afternoon, roundabout noon time with a big kettle and dish out either some soup or something that they would put in the bowl. And so -- and then of course we were -- we were able to get parcels through the mail from our parents. And then we also got parcels from the Red Cross. Parcels and rather than individuals keeping their own, we just took care of each other because there were ten of us guys in this one room. So we just took everything and put it in what we called our pantry. And from there we would make meals.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was in those parcels?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, there was Spam. Crackers. And some powdered milk. A can, you know, about so big and about so high powdered milk. Actually it was called KLIM, milk spelled backwards. And I think there was -- there was coffee in there, I believe. Ground regular coffee. Ground coffee. And oh, crackers and some spread, like sandwich spread. I forget what it was. And a can of corned beef. I recall that. And then there was some -- some of these candy bars, which were -- I forget what they were called. But I guess they tasted like Hershey bars. Something like that. They were intended to be like more of a -- something -- something to give you -- to replenish your vitamins. I don't know whether they had vitamins in it but something that would maybe sustain you better. So anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do to pass the time in the camps?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, fortunately, the American Red Cross would furnish us -- they furnished us with Red Cross parcels and that's where we got the Spam and that stuff. And the Germans did give us, well, we got blood sausage. Have you ever had blood sausage?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, it's it was evidently made out of blood somehow. And -- I never ate it. And it was kind of dark, kind of call it like a maroon color. And it was well jelled so you could slice it. But I had no desire to eat any of it. Like I mentioned, crackers, Spam, powdered milk. I guess we had coffee in there, too. Because we did have coffee. I forget what else. Of course the candy bars. Actually they were, I think, candy bars similar to what sea rations used to have.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever get any news about what was going on in the war?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Oh, yes, uh-huh. We had -- evidently somebody had built a radio. And every room -- not every room, I should say every building -- I forget how many rooms were in the building, but there was one guy who used to be like the fellow to go to for information. And whether he had a radio, I don't know. But then he would come back and he would go to each room and report as to what the allies had done or what was happening. So we did get news that way. We had some idea of how the war was going. And that was about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were the guards like at the camps?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, they had around the camp, of course, barbed wire. The fence and then barbed wire. And then at certain places, at the corner and other places, there used to be these elevated guard houses. We used to call them goon boxes. We called the German guards "goons." Oh, something else. There was one fellow that used to come and do the count. And his name was Holingdal (ph). And ________ he was quite a character. Kind of a nice guy. And of course if you didn't abide by the regulations, you know, they let you know about it. But of course, we had one fellow there who was a full colonel and I think there was one guy who was a brigadier general who was in the camp, an American. I don't know, they evidently had been shot down. And so they kind of watched over us. And so me being an officer, why, we were segregated from the servicemen because the Germans viewed -- they put their officers on a pedestal, so to speak. So we were treated -- we were treated better than the American enlisted men. They were in a different camp. They were put in work parties. We didn't have to work. We just -- well, we use to get up in the morning, and stand for what was what was called the "peel". It was a count. And then after that, why we were free to do what we pleased. And so generally what we used to do, we used to exercise. We would walk around like a path around the perimeter of the camp where the fences were. And so we used to get our exercise that way, walking. And then we received sporting equipment through the Red Cross, baseball and -- we even had baseball teams over there. And some of those guys were pretty good. Like this one pitcher, I forget what has name was, but he could really -- well, it was softball, but he could really whip that ball in there. And so we had some entertainment watching them play baseball and then in the fall, why, there was touch football games going on. So there was some bit of entertainment. And I guess a few times we even had a movie. There was a -- well, a building -- like an auditorium, call it that. And we would watch a movie. But that didn't happen very often.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: American movie or German movie?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: American movies. I forget what the movies were that came in there, but it was some entertainment anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there any escape attempts?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yeah, not in our compound, but in a British compound. Well, there was tunneling work going on always. And what they used to do to get rid of the dirt, they had some kind of a pocket inside their pants here I guess and then they would take a walk around the perimeter and they had a string they would pull and the stuff dropped out. Because, you know they couldn't take the dirt from the tunnel and pile it outside. The Germans would get wise. And it was the British compound. They were all British, either RAF and RCAF fliers, why, there were a number of them that escaped but they were picked up later and the Germans shot them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many were shot?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: I forget, but I believe there was 14 of them, something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It says here 24 March. Could this be right? You were shot down after D-Day; right?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Oh, yes, yeah, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, no. This is something you heard. You heard of the 24 March, 1944, escape of 76 British prisoners and 50 were executed.

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Okay, yeah, uh-huh. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that had happened before you got to that camp?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: I do believe so, uh-huh. But what they had done, they had tunneled out. And of course we had to stand on what was called the peel countdown twice a day in the morning and then in the evening. So if anybody goes missing, why, then they would know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, in at the end of the war, you mentioned that Hitler ordered all prisoners executed; correct?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yes, but the German hierarchy, the Luftwaffe, or whatever army, why, they said no. We're not gonna do it, which they didn't. And instead, why -- whatever what happened to Hitler, I guess he was -- I don't know if he was shot or killed in his bunker where he was hiding. However it was, but no, we were not -- nobody was executed. The only execution I know of were those RAF guys, yeah. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you were in camp in Moosberg when this order came down?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Probably. I think so because would have been towards the end of the war, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any abuse of the prisoners in any of the camps where you were, by the guards?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Any?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Abuse of any sort?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Not to my knowledge. I was not in the camps we were in. Now, in the enlisted area, I don't know what transpired to them as far as abuse or whatever. That may have been the case. I know several people, fellas from around here who were prisons of war. Mel Peltama (ph), he lives in _________ now. He was a Fairport boy. And he was a mouthy guy. And always was, before he was in service. So I don't know maybe he got a little whacking around by the guards when he was there. And then there was Bob Melacovski (ph). I knew him. He was from Hanesville, and there was another fellow from __________. He was at the same camp I was in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you make any close buddies in the camp?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, sort of, yeah, in a way. But then of course when we were liberated, everybody went their own way. So I don't know whether -- well, I guess I did when I went down to Miami Beach for that R&R, well, I did run into a few of them down there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there just officers in the camp where you were, or were you --

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the enlisted men were in a totally separate camp?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yes, because that's the way -- well, the Germans were very, you might say class conscious. And their officers were high muckety-mucks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there Luftwaffe guards at the camp where you were?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yes, they were -- well, I don't know now whether they were Luftwaffe. They may have been because they had a lot of Air Corps people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So they had specific Air Corps prison camps?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you mentioned that you got some letters from home?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were in the camp, what kinds of things would they write to you?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, they would just write to you to let know us about what was going on at home, more or less because some of these letters, I guess they have to be on a certain form. And I guess the letters they were checked over by the Germans and there would be some areas cut out of them. That was something that they didn't want us to know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able to write much back to folks at home?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yeah, we were -- we were able to write, but I don't know that -- how long it took them to arrive there. I'm sure they took awhile, you know. And I am trying to think of how often we had a chance to write. Because see we didn't -- we didn't have the stationery. I think there were forms that were furnished by the Red Cross and similar to what we received. And just write a very -- just exactly how much of that information got back to our parents is hard telling.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war is there any particular vivid memory come to mind that you haven't talked about yet? Either before or after you were captured?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, nothing -- nothing -- well, I guess one of the more happy moments was which we saw the U.S. flag go up the flag pole in our camp. And so we were liberated then. And, then of course Patton's army came through there then. Unfortunately, I didn't see George, but we knew that he had come through there and liberated us. And I guess it was one of the happier moments when we left the camp and knew we were going home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you got home, did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. Maybe; maybe not. Maybe not too much, I don't think. Because, well, of course I didn't do anything for a while. I just lived a life -- a life of leisure, so to speak. And -- because I think I was still getting paid up to a certain time, because -- I forget what it was called. Based on the number of years of service, you know, they paid you some extra money there at the end. And then I got a job and then I decided I better go to school. Because I was working at the Diamond Alkali. Back then Diamond Alkali, that was a busy, big place hiring about 3,000 people over there. And I didn't want to work there all my life. So anyway a lot of the fellas coming home from service, they took advantage of the, you know, college. And so I was able to get four years free of charge, plus I was getting a stipend every month. And then when I was in POW camp, my monthly payments, which would have been my Air Force pay, were being sent home and my parents were banking it for me. So when I went to college, I had enough money, I bought myself a new car. Of course back then, cars didn't cost like they cost now, but of course I didn't have very much money either.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I am guessing you were liberated before VE-Day; is that right?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any of the celebrations on VE-Day?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Yes, as a matter of fact I was home on VE-Day. And I think I was -- I had gone to Geneva Lake on that evening with some buddies of mine and everything was closed up. The dance hall was closed, all the beer joints were closed. Everything was -- was kind of sad in a way, you know? You expect to go somewhere and have some entertainment. But that was all right. And then of course, why, afterward, everything was okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about VJ-Day?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Well, I don't know just what -- I guess I was still at home at that time. And I remember seeing the proceedings on TV when they were -- whether they were right then and there or they were taped. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else? Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Edmund Kuivila
sp.p: Pretty much so. [End of Interview.]
